“Satan’s little season”: are we in it?

Revelation 20 says Satan is bound for a thousand years, then released for a little while. Where each reading places that season, the enemy’s four names, the final battle decoded, and why evil remains.
“Satan’s little season”: are we in it now?
A popular theory says the world now lies under a demonic deception we can only wait out, Satan’s “little season” of Revelation 20. Does the chapter teach that?
Where the idea comes from
It joins two verses: Satan is bound for a thousand years, then released “for a little while” to deceive the nations.
Ask the five questions first
John wrote to seven real churches in Asia, from Patmos, about things that must soon take place. He had heard Jesus' warnings on the Mount of Olives.
“A thousand” means fullness
God owns the cattle on a thousand hills and remembers his covenant for a thousand generations. The number speaks of a complete span set by God, not a count of days.
Bound by Christ
Jesus bound the strong man and plunders his house; at the cross the ruler of this world was cast out, so the gospel could reach the nations.
Gog, the city and the fire
Gog and Magog come from Ezekiel 38-39. Armies surround the beloved city and fire from God consumes them, the prophets' picture of judgement.
Crushed under the church's feet
Paul promised the Roman Christians that God would soon crush Satan under their feet. The devil is a defeated enemy to resist, not a ruler to wait out.
The strong man bound
Christ's ministry, cross and ascension.
Revolt and war
Rome's armies move against Judea.
The beloved city falls
Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed.

Readers who place the little season in AD 66-70 point to Revelation's time words and to armies surrounding the city, as Jesus foretold. Most postmillennial and amillennial readers instead see the thousand years as the whole present age, with a brief rebellion just before Christ returns; premillennialists place it after a future thousand-year reign.

Whatever its timing, the little season is short, limited, and ends in Satan's total defeat. Nothing in Revelation 20 tells the church to sit helplessly under deception; it is sent to make disciples and overcome evil with good.

Partial preterists differ on the timing: many place the thousand years across the present age and the brief release at its end, before the final judgement. Treating the great white throne as already past is a full-preterist view outside the creeds. Scripture also presents the devil as a real, personal enemy, not only a mindset.
